items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: We live in the era of entrepreneurship, the solo enterprise, the gig economy, the individual contributor, etc. There’s been a shift over the last five to 10 years that places a premium on individual autonomy and flexibility. Workplaces are scrambling to catch up with this new normal, including retention of their current team members.

But going it solo can be a lonely place! While some thrive on it, others are forsaking the world of freelance and contractorship only to re-plug into the dynamic of a team. Many employees never left in the first place and are wondering if their current environment can hold up to the ideals of culture, loyalty, and sense of shared accomplishment that we all crave when we join a company.

Pat Summitt was no stranger to the power of team. Not only did she excel in taking freshmen athletes from vastly different backgrounds and turning them into well-oiled championship machines, she went beyond the traditional requirements of a functioning team with her infamous Definite Dozen. Coach Summitt embraced these unique principles as the 12 requirements for success in any organization, including the teams she coached.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: As we learned in the previous course, all 12 of these principles are important. But now it’s time to take a closer look at one of the bedrocks of the modern workforce that seems to erode with each passing year — one that is still vital to a well-oiled organization and the overall health and satisfaction of those who work there: The Power of Team.

items.heading: Why Is the Concept of Team More Important Than Ever?

items.paragraph:
You’ve heard the old saying, “People don’t leave jobs, they leave leaders.” It could equally be said that people don’t leave missions, they leave dysfunctional teams. 

Show me a person who is healthy, functional, plugged in to an organization’s overall mission — someone who truly enjoys working with their fellow team members and feels valued by the organization — and I’ll show you someone who is harder to entice away for a few thousand dollars more per year. These people aren’t even looking elsewhere. It’s the team member who feels isolated, undervalued, and disconnected from the overall mission who is looking over the fence for greener pastures.

So how do you build great teams? Pat would be the first to tell us that people aren’t born great team players. “Teamwork does not come naturally,” she once noted. “How do you convince a group of highly talented individual performers to set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a unified effort?”1 As a coach, it was a problem she personally faced on an annual basis.

items.name: – Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: Teamwork does not come naturally. How do you convince a group of highly talented individual performers to set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a unified effort?”

The truth is, not everyone grew up playing sports where we were taught the power of team. It’s not a skill you necessarily learn in school, as academic performance is up to one’s individual efforts. By contrast, some people grew up playing on dysfunctional teams or participating in extracurricular activities where there were only one or two stars and everyone else on the team was merely an accessory. Yet, if people were honest, it’s the very thing most of us crave — to join with others in pursuit of a healthy, fulfilling mission.

items.heading: The Concept of Team Involves More Than Output

items.paragraph:
The goal of Pat’s championship programs wasn’t to develop star players; it was to have an unbeatable team year after year. “Team-building starts by recruiting good people and turning them into willing role players early on,” she taught.

Self-discipline, responsibility, hard work, and individual performance may come naturally to some, but how do you teach shared ownership, respect for others, loyalty, good communication, respect for the leader, and no gossip, just to name a few?

While all the Definite Dozen principles are important, there are three principles in particular whose lack arguably causes a majority of the problems for teams in the modern workforce.
Click to expand and complete this element.

items.title: Responsibility
items.description: How do you encourage your employees to take ownership for their work and embrace/internalize the shared vision of the company?

items.title: Loyalty
items.description: How do you cultivate employees who are loyal to the company and its mission?

items.title: Communication
items.description: Organizations move at the speed of communication and trust. How do you foster team communication — from the top down, from the bottom up, and from side-to-side among peers?

items.paragraph: There’s a reason these are principles #2 to #4 on the Definite Dozen(c) wheel. We’ll call them the LCR (Loyalty, Communication, Responsibility) of team-building.

items.name: – Pat Summitt
items.paragraph: Team-building starts by recruiting good people and turning them into willing role players early on.”

items.heading: How Do You Develop Winning Teams by Mastering LCR?

items.paragraph: In the upcoming modules, we’ll take a closer look at these three Summitt principles, specifically:
How to encourage responsibility in your team members
How to take responsibility for your area (without micromanaging)
How to be an excellent communicator
The right balance of positive/negative communication
How to show loyalty to your team
How to be a leader employees will never want to leave
And more!

items.paragraph: But first, let’s take a look at some reflections and exercises around the concept of team.

items.heading: Exercises
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.
What are your three biggest obstacles or questions around the concept of team?
How would you like to grow more as the leader of the team? Take five minutes and jot your thoughts in your workbook.

course.description: Whether you’re leading a team of five or 50, this course is designed to help you unlock one of the most powerful forces in leadership…teamwork! As you begin this journey, you’re stepping into something bigger than an online program; you’re stepping into a legacy. Inspired by Coach Summitt’s championship-level ability to bring people together toward a shared goal, the following lessons will guide you through practical strategies and mindsets that build trust, inspire collaboration, loyalty and overall success for your team. Let’s get started!
